abstract: Orchids are a large and diverse group of plants with unique adaptations that have enabled the utilization of many different environmental habitats across almost all continents. These adaptations are mediated by an as-yet-underexplored genetic resource. Nearly all sequenced orchid genomes are of Asian origin and represent less than 0.1% of all orchid species, limiting the ability to explore and mine the gene space of this complex plant family. Greater representation of orchids in genome databases could provide important insights into the genes responsible for adaptive phenotypes, which could be useful for targeted crop improvement and in orchid conservation efforts. To begin to expand the palette of orchid genomes, an effort was undertaken to sequence the genome of a North American terrestrial orchid, Tipularia discolor. K-mer analysis estimated a haploid genome size of approximately 1.7 Gb, with a high proportion of repetitive sequences. Although a complete genome was not obtained, the implementation of a conservative gene mining approach and the generation of a candidate gene mining pipeline led to the identification of 68 consensus contig objects containing whole or partial genes related to sucrose, trehalose, terpenoid, and phenylpropanoid metabolism. Of note, two bibenzyl synthase homologs were identified with high confidence and clustered with characterized orchid bibenzyl synthases in a CHS/BBS phylogeny, indicating that T. discolor, like its Asian and South American relatives, has the capacity to produce this distinct class of phenylpropanoids. Thus, despite substantial fragmentation, the T. discolor assembly contains sufficient gene space representation for targeted candidate gene discovery. This works lays the foundation for functional characterization of selected candidates and development of a more complete genome assembly for comparative genomic studies.
